name: Phenylpropanolamine
lead: Phenylpropanolamine (PPA) is a sympathomimetic drug related to ephedrine and amphetamine that was long used as a nasal decongestant and as an over-the-counter and prescription appetite suppressant. It was a common ingredient of cold remedies and diet aids.[1][2]

It is mainly a norepinephrine-releasing agent, with weaker dopamine release. Its documented effects include raised heart rate and blood pressure, and it has been rarely linked to hemorrhagic stroke.[1] A 2000 case-control study in the New England Journal of Medicine reported an association between PPA-containing products, including appetite suppressants, and hemorrhagic stroke, and regulators then moved to withdraw it.[3]

In November 2000 the US FDA advised against its use, estimating 200 to 500 strokes per year among users aged 18-49, and it was removed from over-the-counter sale in the following years. Canada withdrew it in May 2001 and Australia by July 2001.[1] It is no longer a mainstream product, though it is sometimes mentioned in weight-loss discussions as a former diet-pill ingredient.

paras: PPA was marketed in over-the-counter and prescription diet products. Studies reported some effectiveness in promoting weight loss,[1] although Grokipedia's AI-generated summary notes that its efficacy for weight loss has been questioned relative to its side effects.[2]
Its larger historical use was as a nasal decongestant, usually combined with other cold-remedy ingredients.[1]

The most-cited human study of PPA is a case-control design that recruited adults aged 18-49 from 43 US hospitals after a subarachnoid or intracerebral hemorrhage, comparing their use of PPA-containing products with controls. The authors set out to test case-report links between PPA products, including appetite suppressants, and hemorrhagic stroke.[3]

Other studies in the evidence base concern pharmacology: in vitro work on ephedrine-related stereoisomers at monoamine transporters,[4] and a review of the vascular effects of trace amines and amphetamines.[5] A Cochrane review of interventions to prevent weight gain after smoking cessation also appears in the literature on appetite-affecting drugs.[6]

Common effects are increased heart rate and blood pressure. Hemorrhagic stroke has been rarely reported, which prompted withdrawals starting in 2000.[1][3] The FDA estimated 200 to 500 strokes per year among younger adult users.[1] Grokipedia reports a relative risk of 16.6 for women who recently started PPA-containing appetite suppressants in the stroke study; this figure comes from an AI-generated summary.[2]

PPA acts largely by releasing norepinephrine, which indirectly activates adrenergic receptors, with weak direct receptor affinity and weaker dopamine release. It is about 100 to 200 times less potent than epinephrine or norepinephrine, has a half-life of about 4 hours, and roughly 90 percent is excreted unchanged in urine.[1][4] Chemically it is a substituted amphetamine and phenethylamine closely related to ephedrine, pseudoephedrine and cathinone.[1]

PPA was first synthesised around 1910 and patented as a mydriatic in 1913. Its blood-pressure effects were studied in the 1920s and 1930s and it was in medical use by the 1930s.[1] After the 2000 stroke study, the FDA advised against use, and OTC sale ended by 2005.[1][3]

Under the US Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act of 2005, PPA is controlled because it can be used to make amphetamine. The 2020 CARES Act requires FDA approval before it can return to the market. It remains available by prescription in Sweden and Germany, and as a veterinary treatment for canine urinary incontinence in the US.[1] India banned human use in 2011, but the ban was overturned later that year.[1]

timeline.event: NEJM hemorrhagic stroke case-control study; FDA advises against use in November.[1][3]
Canada (May) and Australia (by July) withdraw PPA.[1]
FDA removes it from over-the-counter sale.[1]
CARES Act requires FDA approval for return to market.[1]

card.summary: Former OTC decongestant and diet-pill stimulant pulled in the early 2000s after a hemorrhagic stroke link.
card.aka: PPA; norephedrine; Dexatrim and Acutrim ingredient
card.note: Withdrawn in the US, Canada and Australia over hemorrhagic stroke risk.

quick.overview:
Phenylpropanolamine was a stimulant-like ingredient in cold remedies and diet pills such as Dexatrim and Acutrim. Some studies showed weight loss, though its evidence base for that use is modest.

A 2000 case-control study linked it to hemorrhagic stroke, and the FDA, Canada and Australia withdrew it in 2000-2005.
quick.mechanism: It releases norepinephrine from nerve endings, tightening blood vessels in the nose and, at higher doses, acting on the brain to reduce appetite. It also raises blood pressure and heart rate.
quick.risks: Documented harms include raised blood pressure and a rare but serious association with hemorrhagic stroke. It is withdrawn for human use in several countries and is regulated in the US as an amphetamine precursor.
